papers.title: LplA-mediated rescue of lethal myopathy and cardiomyopathy in mitochondrial lipoylation-deficient mammalian caused by Lipt1
papers.abstract: Inherited mitochondrial metabolic disorders impair cellular energy generation and often lead to fatal metabolic crises. Mitochondrial lipoylation defects represent a severe case of such disorders that can lead to lethality but lacks effective treatment so far. In this study, we generated a viable mouse model with muscle-specific deficiency of the lipoyltransferase coded by Lipt1 to provide an in vivo preclinical model that overcomes embryonic lethality. Using this model, we examined a bacterial lipoate protein ligase A (LplA)-mediated gene therapy via adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery. By introducing LplA alongside lipoic acid supplementation, we reconstituted a salvage pathway that bypasses the mammalian endogenous lipoylation pathway. The intervention rescued premature lethality, recovered motor function and reversed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the Lipt1-deficient mouse model. Mechanistically, AAV-LplA reconstitutes mitochondrial protein lipoylation and oxidative phosphorylation in situ. This energetic rescue suppresses phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-Akt hyperactivation, thereby restoring autophagic clearance and subsequently contributing to the recovery of the pathological phenotype. This study established AAV-LplA as a promising gene-delivery strategy for rescuing lethal mitochondrial lipoylation disorders.

papers.title: A candidate HNRNPU-CHD2 RNA-processing axis in neurodevelopmental disease
papers.abstract: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNRNPU, which encodes a nuclear RNA-binding scaffold protein, cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, intellectual disability and brain malformations, but the programs that link HNRNPU dosage to neuronal dysfunction remain poorly defined. We depleted HNRNPU in Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells, profiled gene expression and alternative splicing, intersected the two datasets, and asked which of the resulting genes already carried a neurodevelopmental annotation. Knockdown produced 5,643 differentially expressed genes and 21,728 high-confidence splicing events; 1,222 genes changed at both levels, and two pre-specified neurodevelopmental panel genes were among them: CHD2 and DYRK1A. In K562 eCLIP experiments, 107 reproducible HNRNPU peaks were detected across the CHD2 gene body, and three of the four regulated exons introduce a reading-frame shift whose premature termination codon lies far upstream of the final exon junction, predicting nonsense-mediated decay. Public K562 knockdown data reproduced the rise in CHD2 mRNA and the same skipped-exon change, and CHD2 depletion in the neural line SH-SY5Y altered cell-cycle, DNA-repair and neural gene programs. HNRNPU therefore constrains a frameshift-prone splicing switch in CHD2, a candidate route from HNRNPU haploinsufficiency to loss of functional CHD2 if these transcripts are degraded.

papers.title: Putative biosurfactants from polar microbial consortia
papers.abstract: Biosurfactants (BS) are amphiphilic microbial metabolites that are biodegradable, low in toxicity, and environmentally compatible, making them attractive for applications in food, pharmaceutical, and bioremediation industries. This study investigated the phylogenetic composition and biosurfactant-producing potential of marine oil snow (MOS)-associated microbial consortia from the Churchill Marine Observatory, western Hudson Bay. MOS aggregates were cultivated in mineral Bushnell-Haas (BH) medium supplemented with 3% (w/v) NaCl, using motor oil as the sole hydrocarbon source. Enrichment cultures capable of growth in BH medium were subsequently evaluated for biosurfactant production using qualitative and quantitative assays at 4 {degrees}C and 20 {degrees}C. All cultures were maintained as enrichment consortia throughout the study. A total of eight enrichment cultures were identified as biosurfactant-producing consortia. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Pseudoalteromonas dominated all consortia, while Paraglaciecola, Marinomonas, and other taxa were present at varying relative abundances. Although none of the consortia exhibited high emulsification activity (E24 > 40%), biosurfactant yields were significantly higher at 4 {degrees}C. Additionally, three consortia tested positive for rhamnolipid-type biosurfactant production.

papers.title: Organelle Aging Predicts Human Disease
papers.abstract: Aging affects cellular organelles differently, but whether subcellular aging predicts human disease remains unknown. Here, we integrated organelle-enriched proteins in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid proteomes from 61,931 individuals to model aging of 10 organelles across the human lifespan. Organelle aging was heterogeneous with lysosomes, plasma membranes, and Golgi compartments accelerating rapidly after age 60. Individuals with four or more prematurely aged compartments exhibited up to 22-fold higher kidney disease risk and up to 8-fold higher mortality risk. Major diseases are characterized by distinct organelle aging signatures and disease risk increased with the number of accelerated organelles. APOE-{varepsilon}4 dosage was associated with lysosomal and mitochondrial aging and reduced PDP1 levels, implicating altered energy metabolism. Decomposition of organelle signature coefficients into biological programs further showed that diseases are associated with distinct subcellular patterns. These findings establish organelle-resolved aging as a measurable dimension of human biology, revealing subcellular mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility and resilience.

papers.title: Accumulation of two distinct alleles causes astringency loss in cultivated polyploid persimmon
papers.abstract: Persimmon fruit accumulates high levels of proanthocyanidins (PAs), causing extreme astringency. In pollination-constant and non-astringent (PCNA) cultivars, PA accumulation ceases early in fruit development. Although the PCNA trait is recessively controlled by the ASTRINGENCY (AST) locus, its causal gene has remained unknown. Using haplotype-resolved forward genetics in a hexaploid genetic background, we identified the previously uncharacterized TANNIN (TAN) as the causal gene. Long-read sequencing revealed that PCNA originated through the accumulation of independently derived ast alleles that cause transcriptional deficiency of TAN. These findings resolve the complex genetic basis of natural astringency loss in persimmon and provide a framework for molecular breeding. Further investigation of TAN function would uncover mechanisms underlying massive accumulation of PAs in persimmon fruit and insight into specialized metabolite sequestration.

papers.title: The self-renewing lymphoid-biased hematopoietic stem cells support long-term lymphopoiesis in mice
papers.abstract: Lymphopoiesis is profoundly impaired during ageing largely due to ageing-susceptible changes of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). How to maximize the preservation of lymphopoiesis during ageing remains unknown and whether there exists a specific population with life-long lymphoid potential not intensively affected by ageing is of substantial scientific and translational significance. Here, we identified a self-renewable, lymphoid-biased hematopoietic stem cells (Ly-biased HSCs) subset within the EPCR+CD150-CD48-LSK (HSC2) population, phenotypically termed EPCR+MPP6 (CD34-CD135-HSC2), that not only displayed comparable multi-lineage potential with HSC in young mice, but also maintained similar lymphoid-biased reconstitution during aging. The lymphoid-biased characteristics of EPCR+MPP6 were also supported by immune associated program at transcriptome and proteomic levels. Notably, EPCR+MPP6 and HSCs rarely generated one another following the first cell division in vitro and under homeostasis in vivo indicating the most likely independent relationship between them and an earlier-than-thought bifurcation of the lymphoid differentiation pathway, which may function as a backup source to support lymphopoiesis. Collectively, this newly defined Ly-biased HSCs represent a promising cellular target for both mechanistic studies and therapeutic strategies concerning age-related immune decline.

papers.title: A comparative analysis of BrdU and EdU genotoxicity shows that trypanosomatids exhibit unique responses to the presence of these thymidine analogs in their DNA
papers.abstract: The thymidine analogs 5-bromo-2'-deoxyuridine (BrdU) and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) are widely used to monitor DNA synthesis. Although studies have reported EdU toxicity in certain cell types, no reports to date describe genotoxic effects associated with BrdU/EdU use in trypanosomatids, etiological agents of neglected tropical diseases. This lack of studies raises two possibilities: either these nucleotides are not toxic to these parasites, or the observed genotoxicity was not relevant under the experimental conditions used. Here, we assessed the potential toxicity of BrdU and EdU across three pathogenic trypanosomatids: Trypanosoma cruzi, Trypanosoma brucei, and Leishmania major. Our findings show that EdU has greater genotoxic potential than BrdU. Nevertheless, trypanosomatids respond markedly differently to DNA alterations caused by this analog: T. cruzi cells stop replicating and accumulate in S phase, T. brucei tolerates the DNA lesions generated, while part of the L. major population appears to display an altruistic behavior that benefits the survivors. Furthermore, in silico assays suggest that, once incorporated into DNA, the ethynyl group increases the EdU's polarity, thereby altering DNA structure more strongly than BrdU does after the first round of DNA replication. Together, our findings suggest that using thymidine analogs in trypanosomatids should be preceded by rigorous preliminary analysis, especially when using EdU. Otherwise, the data may be biased by a BrdU/EdU-triggered DNA damage response. We believe this study may serve as an atlas to guide the initial selection of thymidine analog concentrations and exposure periods.

papers.title: Tandem repeats in methanogenic archaea and their viruses reveal a shared potential for rapid genomic diversification
papers.abstract: Methanogenic archaea drive global methane emissions, yet the molecular basis of their physiological flexibility is unclear. Archaeal adaptation is typically attributed to horizontal gene transfer, which is episodic and cannot explain rapid, reversible change. Here we show that direct tandem repeats (TRs) offer an intrinsic alternative. By screening 50,567 prokaryotic genomes, we find TR densities in Methanosarcina more than 30-fold above the prokaryotic average, paralleling Borg extrachromosomal elements. These TRs recur at conserved loci while sharing almost no sequence identity between strains, indicating independent origin, and evolve during routine cultivation. Methanogen TRs are transcribed, show ribosome occupancy, and lie near regulatory and cofactor-related genes, whilst being depleted around core energy-conserving and translational machinery. Genic TRs generate intrinsically disordered regions in proteins carrying nucleotide-binding, protein-protein interaction and cell-surface domains, and occur in structural and surface proteins of methanogen-infecting viruses. TRs are therefore an overlooked source of variability and adaptation potential in methanogens and their viruses.

papers.title: Simulating the dynamics of gene regulatory systems at cellular scale
papers.abstract: The temporal nature of eukaryotic gene expression is the result of a complex, non-linear, dynamical system of regulatory processes. So far, models of such systems trade realism for tractability by using strict simplifying assumptions. These simplified models are often unfaithful to our biological understanding; however, without such simplifications, analytical solutions become more challenging and these dynamical systems must then be studied through simulation. Here, we explore the question of how this complex web of gene regulatory connections can be faithfully simulated for all tens of thousands of genes that usually define a eukaryotic organism. We present a proof-of-principle model and simulator, GeneRegulatorySystems.jl which is based on a biophysical chemical master equation that overcomes three key restrictions. First, it allows an exact stochastic simulation of fully non-linear gene expression dynamics, including feedback control, to parsimoniously capture cause and effect relationships of gene regulation. Further, it includes a general framework for implementing diverse mechanisms of gene control such as protein mediated degradation, RNAi, and protein complex formation. Finally, it scales realistically to tens of thousands of genes. We achieve this by introducing a domain-specific programming language to aid the design of experimental protocols from small-scale, well-studied, scenarios of gene regulation inspired by dynamical systems biology up to large-scale, single cell omics experiments with interventions. In this way, our framework provides a grammar of in silico experimental design that can capture single-cell gene expression dynamics for entire genomes.

papers.title: KaryoTap-based scDNA seq assessment of aneuploidy induction by hydroquinone in hematopoietic stem cells
papers.abstract: Monosomy 7 is a frequent cytogenetic alteration associated with poor outcomes in myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia. The benzene metabolite hydroquinone (HQ) has been reported to induce chromosome 7 loss in cultured hematopoietic cells, suggesting a mechanism linking benzene exposure to these diseases. However, these findings were largely based on FISH analysis of selected chromosomes in relatively small numbers of cells. Here, we tested whether HQ increases aneuploidy in primary human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) using KaryoTap, a single-cell DNA sequencing approach that measures copy number across all 22 autosomes, together with interphase FISH. We first identified 20 uM as the highest HQ concentration tested that preserved sufficient viable cells for single-cell analysis. We then examined cord blood and adult mobilized CD34+ cells, including the MPS1 inhibitor reversine as a positive control in the cord blood experiment. Reversine increased whole-chromosome gains and losses, including those of chromosome 7. HQ did not produce a reproducible increase in aneuploidy across three donors and two sources of CD34+ cells, including two concentrations and two timepoints in the adult donor. A modest increase in chromosome 7 loss in one cord blood donor was not reproduced in the other donors. In the other cord blood donor, the estimated upper bound on the HQ-associated increase was approximately 1.4 percentage points. HSPCs also showed a greater increase in chromosome losses than epithelial cells or melanocytes following the same reversine exposure. These findings do not support a substantial, reproducible increase in whole-chromosome aneuploidy after HQ exposure under the conditions tested. They are consistent with a model in which benzene exposure favors the expansion of pre-existing monosomy 7 clones, although this possibility requires direct testing.

papers.title: AMD1-driven MTA production sustains chemoresistance by rewiring PMN-MDSC immunosuppression
papers.abstract: Chemoresistance reflects both tumor cell-intrinsic adaptation and remodeling of the immune microenvironment. However, the mechanisms by which chemoresistant tumor cells orchestrate and sustain an immunosuppressive microenvironment remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that chemoresistant tumors exhibit marked accumulation of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs), which exert potent immunosuppressive effects on CD8+T cells and are critical for drug resistance. Metabolomic profiling reveals that resistant tumor cells release the metabolite 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA). MTA enhances the immunosuppressive function of PMN-MDSCs by bolstering JAK-STAT3 signaling. Mechanistically, MTA binds to the protein tyrosine phosphatase PTPN2 to block its phosphatase activity, thereby potentiating activation of JAK-STAT3 signaling pathway. Moreover, we uncover that adenosylmethionine decarboxylase 1 (AMD1) is the key metabolic determinant of MTA accumulation in chemoresistant tumor cells. Genetic or pharmacological AMD1 inhibition significantly decreases MTA level, diminishes PMN-MDSC immunosuppressive function, and re-sensitizes the resistant tumors to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Our findings identify MTA as an important metabolic link between chemoresistant tumor cells and PMN-MDSCs to sustain immunosuppression and therapeutic resistance. Targeting AMD1-dependent MTA production represents a valuable strategy for overcoming chemo-immunotherapy resistance.

papers.title: Apelin signaling controls neuroendocrine homeostasis via Atoh8-dependent transcriptional regulation
papers.abstract: Apelin is a pleiotropic peptide hormone with established roles in cardiovascular function, angiogenesis, and metabolism, but its contribution to neuroendocrine development and function remains poorly understood. Here, using genetic loss-of-function and inducible gain-of-function approaches in zebrafish, we show that Apelin signaling is dosage-sensitive and required for normal development, reproductive capacity, and physiological homeostasis. Both apelin deficiency and apelin overexpression disrupted embryonic development and reduced adult lifespan, while exhibiting markedly reduced fertility in both sexes. Transcriptomic profiling revealed broad changes in neuroendocrine, hormonal, stress-response, and inflammatory genes with young adult mutant expression profiles resembling those of aged wild-type fish. Both loss and excess of Apelin also disrupted hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis development, reducing hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone-expressing cells, pituitary gonadotropic cell populations, and thyroid gland volume. Transcriptomic analyses identified atoh8, encoding a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, as a candidate effector of Apelin signaling. Apelin expression increased atoh8 expression during early embryogenesis, whereas atoh8 mRNA partially rescued developmental defects in apelin mutants, including hypothalamic and pituitary markers, and thyroid volume. Conversely, atoh8 crispants displayed thyroid and pituitary abnormalities, supporting a role for Atoh8 in neuroendocrine development. Together, these findings establish Apelin signaling as a dosage-sensitive regulator of zebrafish development and tissue homeostasis and identify Atoh8 as a functional downstream effector that partially mediates Apelin-dependent HPT axis formation. This work links peptide hormone signaling to neuroendocrine development and provides a framework for investigating its broader contributions to vertebrate physiology, reproduction and aging.

papers.title: Inflammatory proteostasis reprogramming creates a lysosomal bottleneck for microglial aggregate clearance
papers.abstract: Efficient clearance of extracellular protein aggregates by microglia is essential for maintaining brain homeostasis and limiting the accumulation of pathological proteins during neurodegeneration. However, how inflammatory activation affects the ability of microglia to internalize and degrade these aggregates remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory activation impairs the degradation of extracellularly-acquired -synuclein (-Syn) and Tau aggregates while largely preserving their uptake. Mechanistically, Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation induces translational reprogramming and increases intracellular proteostatic demand, while inhibition of protein synthesis restores -Syn degradation without preventing inflammatory Nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-{kappa}B) activation. Despite largely preserved canonical autophagic flux, inflammatory stimulation is associated with reduced expression of lysosomal proteins, including cathepsin D, suggesting insufficient lysosomal adaptation to increased intracellular demand. Consistent with this model, pharmacological activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) restores aggregate degradation, indicating that the impairment can be overcome by enhancing lysosomal function. Supporting its potential relevance to human disease, microglial -Syn deposits in brain tissue from patients with dementia with Lewy bodies show limited spatial association with cathepsin D-positive structures. Together, our findings identify a demand-driven lysosomal bottleneck through which inflammatory activation compromises aggregate degradation without substantially affecting uptake, highlighting lysosomal adaptation as a critical determinant of microglial aggregate clearance during neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Reconstitution of lipid nanoparticle-mediated siRNA transfer across endosomal membrane mimics
papers.abstract: Endosomal escape limits RNA delivery by lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). If escape requires membrane rupture, productive delivery would be intrinsically coupled to membrane damage and its potential toxicity. Here, we establish a cell-free system based on giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) with an early endosome-like lipid composition to dissect the mechanism of siRNA transfer and determine whether it can occur while membrane barrier function is preserved. Acidification promoted LNP-membrane association, lipid redistribution and siRNA translocation into the receiving lumen without detectable dissipation of transmembrane pH gradient. Complementary cryo-electron tomography revealed local interfacial lipid reorganisation without detectable membrane rupture. Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy revealed heterogeneous diffusion of translocated siRNA, consistent with free and lipid-associated species. Pre-formed RNA-lipid complexes exhibited pH-dependent dissociation and heterogeneous diffusion, supporting lipid association as a possible origin of slower luminal diffusion. Serum or apolipoprotein-E preincubation reduced siRNA translocation into the GUV lumen. Together, these findings support a model where siRNA-lipid association facilitates membrane crossing without sustained loss of barrier function. This platform provides a means to dissect LNP-mediated RNA delivery and develop formulations with improved efficacy while limiting membrane damage.

papers.title: Structural Determinants of Ligand-Mediated Hmg2 Mallostery
papers.abstract: The sterol pathway is a conserved eukaryotic process that produces essential metabolites. Hmg-CoA reductase (HMGR) is a key rate limiting enzyme of the sterol pathway and is the most successful clinical target for managing cholesterol levels. However, determination of the structural features that are essential for its regulation remains elusive. Because of the conservation between mammals and yeast, for many years we have studied the structural features of a yeast Hmg2 isozyme of HMGR. Hmg2 is regulated by the mevalonate pathway isoprenoid GGPP. GGPP acts similarly to an allosteric ligand and appears to bind to a specific site on Hmg2, causing Hmg2 to undergo reversible misfolding. Misfolded Hmg2 is then recognized by the protein quality control mechanism known as the HRD pathway. Due to its similarity to allosteric regulation we have termed this ligand-dependent misfolding mallostery. In this work, we systematically probe each residue of the Hmg2 lumenal domain as well as assess the transmembrane domain and lumenal domain as independent domains and use in vivo and in vitro techniques to assess what regions are important for GGPP response. We identified stabilizing mutations within each loop of the lumenal domain but did not find mutants that were completely unresponsive to GGPP. When assessing the transmembrane domain and lumenal domain as two independent structures, we found that only the transmembrane domain responded to GGPP specifically in vitro. Our results suggest that GGPP binding occurs within the Hmg2 transmembrane domain and that the loops in the lumenal domain are required for transducing a mallosteric response to GGPP. Taken together, these data suggest a new model of Hmg2 regulation.

papers.title: DarHTG is a tripartite phage defence system for purine DNA base ADP-ribosylation
papers.abstract: Bacteria evolved a variety of phage defence strategies to combat the constant onslaught of viral threats. DarTG toxin-antitoxin systems provide phage defence by ADP-ribosylation of bases in single-stranded DNA which interferes with viral replication and aborts phage infection. Here, we describe DarHTG, a system widespread among bacteria, that combines DarTG with a non-processive superfamily I helicase functioning as co-toxin for DarT and thereby enabling the ADP-ribosylation of double-stranded DNA. We identified two such DarHTG subclasses which catalyse the ADP-ribosylation of adenosine and guanosine bases, respectively, and reverse these modifications with structurally unique ARH superfamily antitoxins. Thus, DarHTG antitoxins expand the known macromolecular target spectrum of the ARH enzyme class to nucleic acids. These DarHTG systems confer resistance to a broad range of bacteriophages and can be triggered by the highly charged tails of viral single-stranded DNA-binding proteins, which occlude the active site of the ARH antitoxin.

papers.title: Mixing, competence, and commitment set the stability of cell identity
papers.abstract: Cells maintain their identities in the face of molecular noise, yet can change them rapidly when cued. Here, we treat this tension as a problem in the control of a stochastic system. We represent a cell identity as a set of molecular configurations, or microstates, among which cells undergo stochastic transitions, and measure its stability by the effective rate of commitment to another identity, using a Markov model in which committed cells are removed. Mixing, competence, and commitment provide three channels for tuning this rate. They govern microstate transitions, how commitment is distributed among microstates, and the overall speed of commitment, respectively. Control over the effective commitment rate is shared between commitment and mixing in proportions that always sum to one. Interventions with the same effective commitment rate cannot be told apart by survival alone but, given the microstate transition rates, can be distinguished by the fraction of cells in each microstate or by how quickly cells sorted on permissive microstates commit. When competence varies in time, pulsed commitment signalling commits more cells than sustained signalling of equal dose, by an amount that grows with the depth of that variation, whereas with constant competence pulsing gains nothing in the models we studied. This suggests a possible function for pulsatile signalling, such as that of ERK, which the experiments we propose could test. Finally, reanalysing single-cell imaging of mouse embryonic stem cells leaving naive pluripotency, we estimate that cells take about as long to acquire competence as they then wait to commit, and we specify experiments to identify which channel drives this exit.

papers.title: Dissecting the genetic basis of DUS characters in Pakistani wheat varieties
papers.abstract: Distinctness, Uniformity and Stability (DUS) testing is fundamental to varietal characterization and the protection of Plant Breeders Rights (PBRs), but conventional DUS assessment relies predominantly on morphological characteristics whose expression may be influenced by environmental conditions, developmental stage and observer-related variation. Integrating character-specific molecular markers with conventional DUS assessment may therefore improve the reproducibility and genetic resolution of varietal identification. This study investigated the genetic architecture of DUS characteristics in a panel of 102 historical and modern Pakistani wheat varieties using genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Phenotypic variation was evaluated using distribution, correlation and hierarchical clustering analyses, while the germplasm was genotyped using a wheat genotyping-by-targeted sequencing platform. After quality filtering, 21,670 high-quality single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were retained for analyses of genetic diversity, population structure, linkage disequilibrium (LD) and marker-trait associations. Population structure analysis indicated extensive admixture, with cross-entropy supporting K = 9 ancestral components, whereas hierarchical genetic clustering separated the germplasm into five broad groups. The first three principal components explained 8.09%, 7.20% and 5.39% of the total genetic variation, respectively. GWAS using BLINK and FarmCPU identified significant associations for several diagnostically important DUS characteristics. Growth habit was strongly associated with SNP 1B_129176704, with an additional signal on chromosome 5B. Shattering showed its strongest association at 1D_445256324, accompanied by several closely linked SNPs in the same region and a secondary significant locus at 7B_703502819. Flag leaf length was associated with a cluster of SNPs on chromosome 6A, while tiller density showed a major association with 5D_205488820. These findings demonstrate substantial phenotypic and genetic diversity within Pakistani wheat germplasm and identify genomic regions that merit validation as character-specific molecular tools to complement conventional DUS testing and PBR implementation.

papers.title: SMARCA4 MUTATIONS PROMOTE CHEMOTHERAPY RESISTANCE IN T-ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKEMIA THROUGH ALTERED CHROMATIN REMODELING AT AP1-ASSOCIATED REGULATORY REGIONS
papers.abstract: Chromatin remodelers play a critical role in orchestrating chemotherapy responses in cancer cells. Components of the SWI/SNF complex are frequently mutated across cancer types, with the ATPase subunit SMARCA4 among the most commonly altered. In T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), however, SMARCA4 mutations are rare at diagnosis but enriched in relapse samples, suggesting a potential role in therapy resistance. Using isogenic T-ALL cell lines with or without SMARCA4 mutations, we show that mutant SMARCA4 confers resistance to a broad range of chemotherapeutic agents. By combining ATAC-seq and RNA-seq, we demonstrate that SMARCA4-mutant cells display an attenuated transcriptional response to chemotherapy accompanied by impaired remodeling of AP-1-associated regulatory regions linked to stress response. These cells downregulate stress-related genes while maintaining expression programs associated with cellular fitness. Pharmacological inhibition of AP-1 phenocopies this response, further supporting a functional link between SWI/SNF-mediated remodeling at AP-1-associated regulatory regions, AP-1 activity, and chemotherapy sensitivity. Together, our findings indicate that SWI/SNF-mediated remodeling of these regions contributes to an effective chemotherapy-induced stress response, and that its failure provides T-ALL cells with a survival

papers.title: A Deep Phylogenetic Split Between Short- and Long-Wavelength-Tuned Visual Systems in Surgeonfishes (Acanthuridae)
papers.abstract: The light environment, coupled with ecology, is widely thought to drive visual adaptation, creating species-specific visual niches. However, coral reef ecosystems experience continuous spatiotemporal variations in light conditions, and mechanisms such as phenotypic plasticity may be essential for coral reef animals to adjust to such changing sensory requirements. It remains unclear how widespread colour vision plasticity is, or the extent to which ecology and phylogeny drive plasticity in coral reef fishes. Using a comparative transcriptomic approach across 22 species, we aimed to investigate visual plasticity within a prominent coral reef fish family, surgeonfishes (Acanthuridae), in response to changes in the light environment throughout development and across seasons in adults. Surprisingly, we uncovered a deep phylogenetic split (~42 mya) in visual opsin gene expression profiles, with Nasinae expressing a shorter-shifted palette than Acanthurinae, which coincides with the divide between water-column and benthic-feeding modalities during the speciation of their last common ancestor. However, opsin gene expression showed little variation in response to seasonal or ontogenetic shifts in the light environment, nor in the broad functional feeding groups extant species from both subfamilies fall under. Thus, the invariable visual gene expression observed in present-day surgeonfishes appears to be dictated by phylogenetic inertia, despite rapid diversification into a range of ecological niches. This suggests that spectral tuning into two main modalities, short and long, reduces the need for visual plasticity, allowing larger and more mobile coral reef fishes to conduct visually guided behaviours across the entire range of light environments they encounter.

papers.title: Tissue geometry patterns epidermal stem cell fate in murine interfollicular skin
papers.abstract: How tissues maintain spatial patterns of stem cell renewal and differentiation despite continuous cellular turnover remains poorly understood. Here, we show that microscopic undulations of the dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ) are associated with distinct stem cell behaviors in the mouse epidermis. Using longitudinal intravital imaging and quantitative analysis of cell morphology and lineage dynamics, we find that local DEJ curvature predicts the subsequent fate of daughter cells up to three days before mother cell division. Cells residing in concave valleys preferentially produce proliferating descendants, whereas convex ridges are associated with increased differentiation. These spatial biases are reflected in the expression of stem- and differentiation-associated markers and accumulate into differences in long-term clonal expansion. Remarkably, DEJ geometry remains stable for weeks, persisting across multiple generations of epidermal cells. Moreover, human epidermal equivalents grown on devitalized dermis recapitulate the preferential retention of basal layer cells in valleys, indicating that living dermal cells are not required for this spatial organization. Our findings suggest that stable tissue architecture can pattern stem cell fate probabilities across generations, contributing to functional stem cell heterogeneity.

papers.title: Cigarette smoke extract and palmitic acid exposed patient-derived iPS- RPE cells as a model for AMD
papers.abstract: Purpose: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a multifactorial disease in which dysfunction and loss of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells contribute to disease progression. Besides genetics, cigarette smoking and high fat diet are important environmental and metabolic risk factors for AMD and are associated with RPE dysfunction. However, the effects of combined environmental and metabolic stress on AMD-derived RPE cells remain poorly understood. In this study, we used patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RPE (iPSC-RPE) cells to examine the effects of cigarette smoke extract (CSE) and palmitic acid (PA) on RPE cell function. Methods: iPSCs derived from non-AMD and AMD donors were differentiated into RPE cells and characterized based on morphology, RPE-specific marker expression, polarity, gene expression, and barrier function. Mature iPSC-RPE cells were exposed to different concentrations of CSE and PA to determine experimental conditions. Cell death, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-like morphological changes, stress-related gene expression, RPE polarity, TEER, VEGF-A and PEDF secretion, and intracellular lipid accumulation were then evaluated following CSE, PA, or combined CSE and PA exposure. Results: Differentiated iPSC-RPE cells developed typical pigmented, hexagonal morphology, expressed RPE-specific markers, and formed polarized monolayers. Both CSE and PA increased cell death in a dose-dependent manner in the control and AMD-iPSC-RPE, with AMD-iPSC-RPE exhibiting greater susceptibility, particularly those from patients with dry AMD. CSE and PA also induced also induced EMT-like morphological changes and increased the expression of ZEB1, NQO1, and IL8. Furthermore, CSE and PA disrupted the polarized distribution of ZO-1 and Best1, significantly reduced the polarity ratio, decreased PEDF and VEGF-A secretion and increased intracellular lipid accumulation. Combined CSE and PA treatment produced more pronounced effects than either treatment alone in AMD lines. Conclusions: AMD- iPSC-RPE cells, particularly those derived from dry AMD donors, exhibit increased susceptibility to environmental and metabolic stress. Exposure to CSE and PA revealed this vulnerability through alterations in cell survival, stress responses, epithelial morphology, polarity, secretory function, and intracellular lipid accumulation. These findings highlight the effects of CSE and lipid stress on RPE metabolism and underscore the utility of patient-derived iPSC-RPE cells as a model for investigating how environmental and metabolic factors contribute to RPE dysfunction and AMD pathogenesis.

papers.title: RELAY: Relational In-Context Learning for Cellular Perturbation Prediction
papers.abstract: Cellular responses to perturbations vary across multiple experimental variables, such as perturbation identity, cell type, donor, and dose, defining a multidimensional condition space in which each measured population occupies one coordinate. Existing methods predict unmeasured conditions using explicit representations of these variable values, generalizing unseen values therefore depends on the availability and quality of such representations. We present RELAY, a relational in-context model that predicts unmeasured coordinates from measured responses at related coordinates. For each target, RELAY uses measured control--perturbed pairs from conditions that share one or more experimental variables with the target, such as the same perturbation in another cell type. The model receives only which variables are shared, not their values, and uses these demonstrations to predict the target response. We evaluate RELAY on chemical, genetic, and cytokine perturbation datasets under two settings: unseen combinations, where test values are individually observed during training but not in their target combinations, and unseen variable values, where test values are introduced only through context at inference. RELAY outperforms existing in-context methods on unseen variable values and supervised perturbation-prediction methods on unseen combinations. All resources will be open sourced, including code and data.

papers.title: Dual role of RBM3 in PEDV infection: stabilization of viral RNA and upregulation of the entry factor HSPA5
papers.abstract: RBM3, a member of the cold-shock protein family, functions as an RNA chaperone that stabilizes target transcripts by binding to their untranslated regions (UTRs). Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) is an enteric coronavirus that poses a serious threat to the swine industry, and its replication heavily depends on its genomic and subgenomic RNAs, making these RNAs potential targets for host RNA-binding proteins. In this study, we show that RBM3 promotes PEDV replication through a dual mechanism. On one hand, RBM3 exhibits a binding preference for the viral 3'UTR, which prolongs the half-life of viral RNA and thereby promotes PEDV proliferation. RBM3 also interacts with the PEDV nucleocapsid (N) protein and replication-associated double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) signals, suggesting that RBM3 may be associated with viral replication complexes, though its contribution to their functional integrity remains to be determined. On the other hand, RBM3 increases HSPA5 promoter activity and HSPA5 mRNA levels, linking RBM3 to HSPA5, a host factor known to facilitate PEDV attachment and internalization. These two mechanisms together provide a mechanistic basis for efficient PEDV infection. Our findings identify RBM3 as a positive host regulator of PEDV and establish, for the first time, a functional link between RBM3 and HSPA5, offering new insights into coronavirus-host interactions and suggesting RBM3 as a potential target for antiviral intervention.

papers.title: Enzyme-Constrained Metabolic Modeling Reveals CO2-Dependent Growth Control in Picochlorum celeri
papers.abstract: Picochlorum celeri grows 11.6 times faster at elevated CO2 than in air, yet the abundance of its metabolic enzymes is only 17% higher. To explain this, we reconstructed iPiccel954, a genome-scale metabolic model with 3525 reactions, 2973 metabolites and 954 genes, and eciPiccel954, its enzyme-constrained version limited by the measured enzyme abundance in air and at elevated CO2. Calibrating the enzyme-constrained models against the measured proteome showed that a similar protein budget supports very different growth depending on how it is allocated. With urea as the nitrogen source, urea carboxylase was the only step whose relaxation alone raised growth, by 627% in air and 78% at elevated CO2. Bottleneck analysis showed that growth is limited by many enzymes spread across the network in both conditions, that the limiting enzymes differ between the two, and that control over starch metabolism seen in air disappears at elevated CO2. Measured proteomes agreed with these predictions, since the predicted bottleneck enzymes were more abundant than other enzymes. Rapid growth in P. celeri therefore reflects how the protein budget is allocated more than how large it is. Therefore, eciPiccel954 provides a quantitative basis for engineering this alga for biotechnological application.

papers.title: Synthetic reaction-diffusion patterning in mammalian cells
papers.abstract: During development, periodic patterns arise through reaction-diffusion (RD) circuits involving local activation and long-range inhibition (LALI). Natural systems are complex, typically entangling regulation and transport in the same morphogens. It remains unclear what minimal circuits are sufficient for LALI patterning in mammalian cells, and whether they can be implemented in a modular fashion, allowing independent control of regulation and transport. Here, we designed synthetic LALI circuits using three natural and synthetic signaling systems, BMP, Activin, and the SNIPR pathway, and showed that they generate spatial patterns with distinct characteristic spatial scales. Model-guided design allowed flexible morphogen reassignment, with BMP4 acting as either short-range activator or long-range inhibitor. Gene expression noise degraded long-range order but preserved the dominant local spatial scale. Together, these results provide a modular, extensible synthetic framework for engineered patterning in mammalian cells.

papers.title: Biosensor-guided genome-wide CRISPR screens enable cis,cis-muconic acid overproduction in yeast
papers.abstract: Classical pathway metabolic engineering relies on enhancing strain productivity through the introduction of rationally identified genetic perturbations, which while useful, are time-consuming and miss unintuitive targets. Genome-wide CRISPR screens offer an alternative by efficiently sampling genomes, enabling the engineering of novel phenotypes, and are further enhanced when combined with high-throughput strain interrogation methods. Here, using Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we engineered small molecule biosensors into population enrichment tools using zeocin resistance and fluorescence as signal outputs. We then introduced the multi-functional genome-wide CRISPR (MAGIC) library that targets every gene for activation, interference, or deletion, thus creating biosensor-aided MAGIC, or senMAGIC. As a case study, we utilized senMAGIC to identify single genetic determinants that improve productivity of the nylon precursors protocatechuic and cis,cis-muconic acids (PCA and ccM). These were then randomly assembled as triple gRNA-tRNA arrays for multiplexed gene perturbations to identify combinatorial effects. Top gRNA hits were then confirmed using direct genomic integrations in senMAGIC-free production strains, resulting in identifying known as well as novel targets that increase PCA and ccM titres. Our results demonstrate senMAGIC as a robust automation-friendly whole-genome evolution tool and highlight limitations of the method, providing a roadmap for future multifunctional CRISPR screens to optimize host metabolism for efficient bioprocesses.

papers.title: Brazilian bryophytes: a national-scale comprehensive dataset of species richness and geographic distribution
papers.abstract: Bryophytes (Anthocerotophyta, Marchantiophyta, and Bryophyta) remain under-sampled in large-scale biodiversity databases in Brazil, despite their ecological importance. In Brazil, Flora e Funga do Brasil recognizes 1,618 bryophyte species distributed across six biomes that are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic pressures such as deforestation, agricultural expansion, and climate change. Nevertheless, knowledge of species geographic distributions remains fragmented and based on scattered records. Flora e Funga do Brasil serves as the official taxonomic reference for the country, providing the accepted species list and serving as a baseline for biodiversity studies. However, as it was designed as a nomenclatural and taxonomic checklist, it does not integrate primary occurrence records with geographic coordinates and collection dates. Consequently, occurrence data remain dispersed across herbaria, digital repositories, and the scientific literature, without dynamic updates linked to the official checklist. This disconnect between the taxonomic framework and primary occurrence records limits macroecological and biogeographical analyses at national scales, which depend on standardized georeferenced biodiversity databases. To address this gap, we compiled 102,528 bryophyte occurrence records from herbarium specimens, using data from GBIF and the speciesLink network, complemented by field collections from the Caatinga and records from the Cryptogamic Herbarium of the State University of Piaui. All records were georeferenced and curated, including verification of inconsistent coordinates, removal of duplicates, and taxonomic standardization using Bryonames. When available, information such as collection date and collector was retained. The dataset comprises 1,821 species, 125 families, and 442 genera. Bryophyta (mosses) was the most diverse group (1,056 spp., 84 families, 310 genera), followed by Marchantiophyta (745 spp., 37 families, 124 genera) and Anthocerotophyta (19 spp., four families, seven genera). Among mosses, the most species-rich families were Sphagnaceae (79 spp.), Fissidentaceae (76 spp.), and Pottiaceae (76 spp.). Among liverworts, Lejeuneaceae dominated with 335 species, followed by Lepidoziaceae (58 spp.) and Plagiochilaceae (51 spp.). Among hornworts, Anthocerotaceae, Dendrocerotaceae, and Notothyladaceae each included six species. Regionally, the Southeast showed the highest richness (1,338 spp.), followed by the South (974 spp.), Central-West (937 spp.), Northeast (897 spp.), and North (763 spp.). Regarding biomes, the Atlantic Forest (1,523 spp.) and Amazon (1,054 spp.) were the most species-rich, followed by the Cerrado (810 spp.), Caatinga (671 spp.), Pampa (269 spp.), and Pantanal (61 spp.). These patterns reflect both ecological gradients and historical sampling biases. This dataset bridges the gap between the official taxonomic checklist and primary occurrence data by integrating multiple sources into a standardized, openly accessible database. It provides a robust tool for studies in macroecology, biogeography, and conservation, enabling analyses of spatial patterns of species richness, endemism, and taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic diversity across environmental gradients. It also supports species distribution modeling, climate change impact assessments, biodiversity hotspot identification, and conservation planning at regional and national scales. Users are encouraged to cite this article when using the dataset and to report downstream applications derived from it.

papers.title: PSI photoinhibition and protection at low temperatures and in fluctuating light: An 30 ecophysiological vista
papers.abstract: In green leaves in vivo, photosystem I (PSI) was thought to be resistant to photoinhibition. In 1994, it was found that, in chilling-sensitive plants such as cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.), exposing leaves to moderate constant light at temperatures below 10 degrees C induces PSI photoinhibition with little effect on PSII. Since the beginning of this century, PSI photoinhibition induced by fluctuating light (alternating high and low light, FL) or repetitive saturating pulses (rSPs) has been reported in many species. In this review, we compare the causes and consequences of PSI photoinhibition in cucumber at chilling temperatures with those of PSI photoinhibition induced by FL or rSPs. Changes in chloroplasts during these photoinhibitory treatments are followed, focusing on where and how reactive oxygen species are produced and which parts of PSI are damaged. We also discuss the roles of two pathways of cyclic electron flow around PSI, the NDH and PGR5/PGRL1 pathways, particularly in suppression of PSI photoinhibition. Lastly, we discuss problems with methods for measuring PSI parameters and future research directions from an ecophysiological viewpoint.

papers.title: ANABOLIC FAILURE, NOT CATABOLIC ACTIVATION, UNDERLIES GLYCOGEN DEPLETION IN CERVICAL CARCINOGENESIS: A MULTI-COHORT TRANSCRIPTOMIC ANALYSIS
papers.abstract: Abstract Background. Cervical epithelium loses its glycogen as disease grade rises, an observation old enough to underpin iodine-based visual screening, but which arm of glycogen metabolism accounts for the loss has not been established. The expectation from cancer metabolism is catabolic: that stored glycogen is mobilized and glycolysis activated. Methods. We analyzed 238 specimens from four publicly available cohorts across three sample types: 128 laser-capture-microdissected epithelial samples, 35 bulk-tissue samples, and 75 exfoliated cytology samples in two sets (44 and 31; GSE27678). We prespecified a 33-gene panel comprising four modules: glycogen synthesis, glycogen degradation, glycolysis, and squamous differentiation. For each specimen, we calculated module scores using single-sample gene set enrichment. Differential expression was assessed with limma, pathway enrichment with fgsea, and classification performance with bootstrap confidence intervals for ROC curves. We documented all analytical decisions and their rationale. Results. Synthesis and differentiation fell with grade in all four cohorts, while degradation and glycolysis stayed at their normal-tissue baseline. All seven differentiation genes were reduced in carcinoma, and all seven occupied the top 5.1% of the ranked transcriptome, with CRNN the most down-regulated of 21,755 genes. Synthesis failed selectively, through GYS2 and PPP1R3C only, with the ubiquitous synthase GYS1 unchanged. The glycolytic module separated from normal epithelium at no grade (p 0.45 to 0.62), classified CIN3 or worse at an area under the curve of 0.569 with an interval spanning chance, and showed no enrichment in carcinoma. Synthesis separated from normal first, at CIN2, and differentiation at CIN3. The composite index tracked grade in the discovery cohort (Spearman rho 0.652, p 7.9e-17) but offered no discriminatory advantage over its differentiation component alone (0.832 against 0.832). Conclusions. Glycogen depletion in cervical carcinogenesis reflects failure of a tissue-restricted synthetic axis, GYS2 and PPP1R3C, within a collapsing squamous differentiation program, not catabolic activation. Measuring all four candidate mechanisms on one scale in the same specimen is what allows the catabolic explanation to be excluded rather than merely left untested. The pattern holds across two array chemistries and three specimen preparations, including the exfoliated cytology that screening already collects, and the synthesis and differentiation modules together are the molecular counterpart of what iodine staining reports. These are transcript-level findings and define no clinical threshold.
